parole.testo: Attested a few times in Old High German, but only much later effectively introduced via Middle Low German ūster, from Middle Dutch oester. The Dutch word is borrowed from Latin ostrea, itself from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon) (pertaining to ὀστέον (ostéon, “bone”), ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “shell”)).

parole.significato: forecastle (raised part of the upper deck)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bak (“bowl, box, chest”), from Middle Dutch bak (modern Dutch bak), from Old French bac (“large bowl”). Related with Becken, but unrelated with Backbord. The sense “dining table” is due to the fact that several sailors would eat from one bowl, so the word Back came to be used

parole.significato: animal, beast, any kind but especially an annoying one, e.g. an insect, pest, aggressive dog, etc.
parole.testo: Via Middle Low German and/or West Central German from Middle Dutch beest, itself from Old French beste, from Latin bēstia. Doublet of Bestie.
From Middle Low German and Middle Dutch bolwerk.

Spread via the Lower Rhineland from Middle Low German dingesdach, dinsdach and Middle Dutch dinsendach (both with variants), and gradually replaced Middle High German ziestac and other High German forms like Alemannic German Zischtig or Bavarian Ertag. Only since the second half of the 17th. century

parole.significato: box (container made from metal or plastic, less often wood)
parole.testo: Spread via the Lower Rhineland from Middle Low German dōse and Middle Dutch dose. Probably from Latin dosis (“dose”), with semantic shift "a small amount (dose) of medicine" > "a container of such a dose of medicine" > "containers in general".

Seemingly from Middle Low German and/or Middle Dutch drillen, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *þurhil (“perforated, hole”). Via Middle Low German flau, from Middle Dutch vlau (compare modern Dutch flauw). The Dutch word was borrowed from Old French flou (“tired, weary”), which is probably of Germanic origin and, if so, then cognate with German lau.

Ca. 1600, from Middle Low German vlêder, vlider (“elder”), itself probably from Middle Dutch vlieder, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *fleuþr. Cognate with modern Dutch vlier, West Frisian flear. Via Middle Low German from Middle Dutch vlot (“afloat, floatable”). Ultimately from the root of fließen (“to flow”).
17th century, from Middle Low German and Middle Dutch gilde. Related to Geld and gelten, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *geldan (“to pay”).

From Middle High German hantieren, which is borrowed—probably via Middle Low German—from Middle Dutch hanteren, itself from Old French hanter (“to frequent someone”). 16th century, from Middle Low German hāst, from Middle Dutch haest, a borrowing from Old French haste, itself borrowed from Frankish *hai(f)st, from Proto-Germanic *haifstiz. See English haste for more.

From Middle High German kabel, which is borrowed via Middle Low German from Middle Dutch cabel (“thick rope”), itself from northern French câble. The contemporary sense is from English cable, which see for more.

Circa 1600, from Middle Low German kabbelouw (14th c.), from Middle Dutch cabbeliau, cabelliau (12th c.), from Old Dutch cabillau, possibly from Latin baculum (“stick, staff”), referring to the way cod were split and dried on wooden sticks. parole.significato: cabin, sleeping quarters (on a ship, barge, yacht, etc. for passengers and officers)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German kajüte, which is probably borrowed from Middle Dutch kayhute, though the latter is attested somewhat later. Further origin unsettled; traditionally held to be of Old French origin, according to Watkins, possibly a mix of cabane + hutte. Compare modern Dutch kajuit.

parole.significato: cinnamon in the form of sticks; (collective) cinnamon sticks
parole.testo: From northern Middle High German kanēl and Middle Low German kaneel, from Middle Dutch caneel, from Old French canele. Cognate with Dutch kaneel, French cannelle.

From Middle Low German kanīneken, diminutive of kanīn, konīn, itself probably through Middle Dutch connijn from Old French connin, northern variant of connil, from Latin cunīculus. Analysable as Kanin + -chen. Compare English cony.

Via Middle Low German kant, kante from Middle Dutch kant, itself from Latin canthus (“tire, edge of a wheel”), from Gaulish *cantos, from Proto-Celtic *kantos (“corner, rim”). The Latin spelling is influenced by Ancient Greek κανθός (kanthós, “corner of the eye, tire, etc.”).

parole.significato: to cut down so as to make unusable; to cut off; to interrupt
parole.testo: 17th century, from Middle Low German kappen, from Middle Dutch cappen (“to chop”), perhaps a borrowing from Romansh and from Medieval Latin cappare (“to cut off”), from Vulgar Latin *cappo, from Latin capo (“castrated male chicken”). Compare Alemannic German (Alsatian) kchapfen (“to chop, mince”).
From Middle High German klār, clār, formally from Middle Low German klār or Middle Dutch claer and reinforced by Old French cler, both from Latin clārus (“bright”). Doublet of klaro.

parole.significato: rock that is partly covered by (sea) water
parole.testo: From Middle High German klippe, borrowed from Middle Low German klippe or Middle Dutch clippe, ultimately from the root of Kliff (“cliff”). Cognate with Dutch klip, English cliff.

From Middle High German kluoc, which was borrowed via the Lower Rhineland from Middle Low German klōk and Middle Dutch cloec, from Proto-Germanic *klōkaz. parole.significato: cabin; berth (sleeping room on a ship)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German kōje, from Middle Dutch coye, koye, from Latin cavea. Compare Dutch kooi.

parole.significato: trading post, factory (branch office of merchants)
parole.testo: Since 16th century, borrowed from Middle Low German kontôr, kuntôr, kumptôr (“commercial branch; writing room; counting desk”), from Middle Dutch contoor, comptoir (modern kantoor), from Middle French contoir, comptoer, from compter (“to count”) + -oir. See English counter for more.

parole.significato: to tack (manoeuvre a ship through strong winds)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German lavēren, from Middle Dutch laveren, loveren, which is derived from the cognate of German Luv (“windward side of the ship”). Borrowed from Middle Low German mākeler, mēkeler, and Middle Dutch makelare (compare modern Dutch makelaar). From Middle High German makrēle, from Middle Low German makkerēle, from Middle Dutch makereel, from Old French maquerel. Further origin unknown. Compare modern Dutch makreel, modern French maquereau, English mackerel.
Borrowed from Middle Low German mōras, an alteration of Middle Dutch maras on the basis of the predecessor of German Moor (“bog; moor”).

From northern Middle High German and Middle Low German mostert, both from Middle Dutch mostaert, from Old French mostarde. Doublet of Mostrich. Cognate with Luxembourgish Moschter, Dutch mosterd, English mustard, French moutarde.
From Middle Low German panēl, probably through Middle Dutch paneel eventually from Old French panel, from Vulgar Latin *pannellus. Doublet of Panel.
From Middle Low German pîr, from Middle Dutch pier, spread by Dutch settlers during the eastern colonisation.

From northern Middle High German pissen and Middle Low German pissen, by surface analysis, Pisse + -en. Perhaps borrowed through Middle Dutch pissen from Old French pissier, from Vulgar Latin *pīssiāre, probably of echoic origin, though the Germanic words are also sometimes considered independent on
16th century, from Middle Low German pumpe, pompe, from Middle Dutch pompe. Further origin uncertain, but probably onomatopoeic. Compare English pump.
Borrowed from Middle Low German slūse, from Middle Dutch slūse, sluise, from Old French escluse (French écluse).

parole.significato: to hatch (shade an area with fine lines)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German schrafferen, from Middle Dutch schraeffeeren, from Italian sgraffiare (“scratch”).

parole.significato: country, state (politically constituted legal person wielding absolute power of a population and territory)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German stāt, from Middle Dutch staet, probably via Old French estat from Latin status. The semantic development was influenced by cognate modern French état. Doublet of Status and Etat.
Borrowed from Middle Low German staffēren, borrowed from Middle Dutch stoffēren, borrowed from Old French estoffer. Doublet of stopfen and stoppen.

From Middle Low German sūden and Middle Dutch sūden. The form is already attested in Middle High German sūden, which replaces native Middle High German sunden from Old High German sundan. However, the modern form with a preserved monophthong must be directly from Middle Low German or Middle Dutch. T

parole.significato: to feel with the hands, to fumble, to grope
parole.testo: From northern Middle High German and Middle Low German tasten, from Middle Dutch tasten, from Old French taster, from Vulgar Latin *tastare, from *taxitare, from Latin taxare. Cognate with Dutch tasten, French tâter, English taste.

parole.significato: hours, o'clock (indicates the time within a twelve- or twenty-four-hour period)
parole.testo: From late Middle High German ūre, from Middle Low German ûre (“hour”), from Middle Dutch ûre, from Old Dutch *ūra, from Old French houre, from Latin hōra, from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra), from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₁- (“year, season”). parole.significato: side costs that must be added to the estimated main costs or deduced from a profit; costs that only indirectly serve th…
parole.testo: 15th century, from un- + Kosten, literally “un-costs”, i.e. “bad costs” (with the prefix used as in Unmensch). At first Central German, surely after earlier Middle Low German unkost or Middle Dutch oncost (1372).

Since ca. 1500, from univerbation of zu + Frieden, literally “at peace”. Likely a calque of Middle Low German tô vrēde(n), Middle Dutch te vrēden (modern Dutch tevreden), both of which date from the 13th century.
